note: The science refresh's unit list. One unit = one piece of ONE grade's curriculum, in ONE tier. Pilot units carry pilot: true. map_lines are filled from curriculum_map.json.

units.title: Telling Materials Apart
units.scope: Physical properties a 5th grader observes and measures: mass (with a balance), magnetism (iron and steel are pulled by a magnet; aluminium, copper and plastic are not), floating or sinking in water, physical state, volume, solubility in water (salt and sugar dissolve, sand does not), conducting or insulating heat and electricity (metals conduct; wood, plastic, rubber insulate), hardness, colour and shine; identifying a material by its properties.
units.not_here: States of matter in detail and mixtures are separate units.
units.lane_note: Use lab, rock, nature and body examples, not kitchen or cooking ones (the cooking bank owns those).

units.title: Solids, Liquids and Gases
units.scope: The three states of matter: a solid keeps its own shape and volume, a liquid keeps its volume but takes the shape of its container, a gas spreads to fill any container. Water as ice, liquid water and water vapour; melting and freezing at 0 degrees Celsius, boiling at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level; heating melts and boils, cooling condenses and freezes; changing state does not make a new substance.
units.not_here: Particles moving in each state is a T2 unit.
units.lane_note: Use lab, rock, nature and body examples, not kitchen or cooking ones (the cooking bank owns those).

units.title: Matter Made of Tiny Particles
units.scope: Matter is made of particles too small to see. Evidence a 5th grader can try: air fills and shapes a balloon and has mass (a full ball weighs more than a flat one); a smell spreads across a room though nothing is seen; salt or sugar dissolved in water seems to vanish but the water tastes of it and the solid comes back when the water evaporates; 'atom' as the name for these tiny particles.
units.lane_note: Use lab, rock, nature and body examples, not kitchen or cooking ones (the cooking bank owns those).

units.title: Mixtures and Solutions
units.scope: In a mixture each substance keeps its own properties and can be separated: iron filings pulled from sand by a magnet, sand caught by a filter or a sieve, salt left behind when salt water evaporates. A solution is a mixture in which one substance dissolves evenly in another (salt in water). The total mass stays the same when things are mixed, dissolved, melted or frozen. Some mixings make a new substance (the first look at a chemical change).
units.lane_note: Use lab, rock, nature and body examples, not kitchen or cooking ones (the cooking bank owns those).

units.title: Pushes, Pulls and Gravity
units.scope: A force is a push or a pull. Balanced forces leave motion unchanged (a tug-of-war that does not move); unbalanced forces start, stop, speed up, slow down or turn an object. Friction slows moving things and is greater on rough surfaces. Gravity pulls things down, toward the centre of the round Earth, everywhere on Earth. Testing a force with a toy car on a ramp.

units.title: Energy Changes Form
units.scope: Forms of energy a 5th grader names: light, thermal (heat), sound, electrical, mechanical (motion) and chemical (stored in food, fuel and batteries). Energy changes from one form to another: a flashlight turns a battery's chemical energy into electrical energy, then light (and some heat); a fan turns electrical energy into motion; a speaker into sound; a solar panel turns light into electrical energy; most energy on Earth comes from the Sun.

units.title: Electric Circuits
units.scope: A working circuit needs a complete, closed loop: an energy source (a battery), conductors (wires) and a device (a bulb, a buzzer, a motor). An open switch or a break in the loop stops the current. Conductors (copper and other metals) let electricity flow; insulators (plastic, rubber, glass, wood) do not, which is why wires are coated in plastic. A circuit turns electrical energy into light, sound, motion or heat.

units.title: How Light Travels
units.scope: Light travels in straight lines (so shadows have sharp edges and a laser beam is straight). Light is reflected (a mirror), refracted or bent when it passes from one material into another (a straw looks broken in a glass of water; a lens; a prism spreads white light into a rainbow of colours), or absorbed (a black shirt warms in sunlight more than a white one). White light is a mix of colours. We see an object when light from it enters our eyes.
units.not_here: Wave properties and the electromagnetic spectrum are T4.

units.title: How Plants Make Food
units.scope: Plants make their own food (sugar) by photosynthesis, using the Sun's light, water and carbon dioxide from the air, in their leaves; green chlorophyll captures the light; plants give off oxygen; a plant's mass comes mostly from air and water, not from the soil; animals depend on plants for food and oxygen; the energy in food first came from the Sun.
units.not_here: The plant's parts and their jobs are the next unit.

units.title: Roots, Stems, Leaves and Flowers
units.scope: The parts of a plant and their jobs: roots hold the plant in the ground and take in water and minerals; the stem holds the plant up and carries water up and food down through tiny tubes; leaves make food; tiny pores in leaves (stomata) let gases in and out; flowers make seeds; fruits hold and protect seeds; seeds are spread by wind, water and animals; a seed sprouts (germinates) into a new plant.
units.lane_note: Use lab, rock, nature and body examples, not kitchen or cooking ones (the cooking bank owns those).

units.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
units.scope: Producers (plants and algae) make food from sunlight; consumers eat: herbivores eat plants, carnivores eat animals, omnivores eat both; decomposers break down dead things. A food chain shows who eats whom, and its arrows point the way the energy goes; a food web is many chains joined; energy starts with the Sun; predicting what happens when one member of a web disappears or grows in number.
units.lane_note: Teach the general science; one named animal's own anatomy or behaviour is the animal bank's.

units.title: Decomposers and Recycling Matter
units.scope: Decomposers (bacteria and fungi such as mushrooms and moulds) and scavengers and detritus eaters (earthworms, some beetles) break down dead plants and animals and wastes; they return nutrients to the soil, where plants use them again; matter is recycled again and again, while energy flows through once from the Sun; a rotting log and a compost pile as examples; without decomposers dead matter would pile up.
units.lane_note: Teach the general science; one named animal's own anatomy or behaviour is the animal bank's.

units.title: Ecosystems: Living and Nonliving Parts
units.scope: An ecosystem is the living things in a place (biotic factors: plants, animals, fungi, bacteria) together with the nonliving things (abiotic factors: sunlight, water, air, soil, temperature). Living things depend on both; a habitat is where an organism lives and finds what it needs; changes such as drought, pollution or cutting down a forest affect the organisms; people can harm an ecosystem or help restore it.
units.lane_note: Teach the general science; one named animal's own anatomy or behaviour is the animal bank's. Teach the process; named places and landforms are the geography bank's.

units.title: Adaptations: Built for a Place
units.scope: An adaptation is an inherited feature that helps a living thing survive in its environment: body coverings (thick fur or blubber for cold), colouring (camouflage), body parts for food (beak and tooth shapes in general), plants' adaptations (a cactus stores water and has spines instead of leaves; desert plants' long roots; leaves that shed in winter). Adaptations are inherited, not chosen or learned in one lifetime.
units.lane_note: Teach the general science; one named animal's own anatomy or behaviour is the animal bank's. Use kinds of animals and plants in general (desert plants, animals of the cold), not one species' famous trick.

units.title: Born Knowing or Learned
units.scope: Instincts are behaviours a living thing is born able to do, with no teaching (a baby grasping a finger, a spider spinning a web, sea-turtle hatchlings heading for the sea); learned behaviours come from experience or being taught (a child learning to ride a bicycle, a dog learning a trick); both help survival; inherited traits (eye colour) differ from things gained in life (a scar, a skill).
units.lane_note: The question is only inborn or learned, and how it helps; one species' behaviour for its own sake is the animal bank's.

units.title: The Body's Main Organs
units.scope: The human body's main organs and their jobs: the heart pumps blood around the body; blood carries oxygen and food to every part; the lungs take in oxygen and give off carbon dioxide; the stomach and intestines break down food so the body can use it; the brain is the control centre and nerves carry its messages; bones support and protect (the skull guards the brain, the ribs the heart and lungs); muscles move the bones; the skin covers and protects.
units.lane_note: Keep it clinical and simple; no reproductive system.

units.title: The Sun and Its Planets
units.scope: The Sun is a star, the closest one to Earth, and the centre of the solar system; it gives Earth light and heat. The eight planets in order from the Sun. The four inner rocky planets and the four outer giant planets. Mercury is closest; Jupiter is largest; Saturn's bright rings; Mars looks red (rusty dust); Venus is the hottest planet (its thick air traps heat) and the brightest planet in our sky; Earth is the only planet known to have life and liquid water on its surface. The Moon orbits Earth and shines by reflected sunlight. The Sun's gravity keeps the planets in orbit. Earth goes once round the Sun in about 365 days (a year). The asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter. Pluto is now called a dwarf planet.
units.not_here: Day and night, the Moon's phases, seasons and shadows are separate T1 units; do not ask them here.

units.title: Day, Night and Shadows
units.scope: Earth spins on its axis once about every 24 hours; that spin makes day and night (the side facing the Sun has day); the Sun seems to rise in the east and set in the west because Earth turns; a shadow forms where an object blocks light; shadows are longest in the early morning and late afternoon and shortest near midday, and they point away from the Sun; the Sun does not move around Earth.
units.not_here: Seasons and the Moon's phases are T2 units.

units.title: The Water Cycle
units.scope: The Sun's energy evaporates water from oceans, lakes and puddles into water vapour; the vapour rises, cools and condenses into tiny droplets that make clouds; water falls as precipitation (rain, snow, sleet, hail); it collects in oceans, lakes, rivers and underground (groundwater) or runs off the land; the same water goes round and round. Nearly all of Earth's water (about 97 percent) is salt water in the ocean; most fresh water is frozen in ice caps and glaciers or underground.
units.lane_note: Teach the process; named places and landforms are the geography bank's.

units.title: Wind, Water and Ice Shape the Land
units.scope: Weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces (water freezing in cracks, plant roots, wind-blown sand); erosion carries the pieces away (by water, wind, ice and gravity); deposition drops them somewhere else. What these build and carve: a river cuts a canyon over a long time, drops sediment where it meets the sea (a delta), wind heaps sand into dunes, glaciers carve U-shaped valleys; fast changes too (landslides, floods).
units.lane_note: Teach the process; named places and landforms are the geography bank's.

units.title: Rock Layers and Fossils
units.scope: Sediment (bits of rock, sand, mud and shells) settles in layers; over a long time the layers are pressed and cemented into sedimentary rock (sandstone, shale, limestone); most fossils are found in sedimentary rock; a fossil is the remains or traces of a living thing from long ago (bones, shells, footprints, imprints of leaves); fossils show what places were like long ago (sea shells in rock on dry land mean a sea was once there); coal, oil and natural gas formed over millions of years from buried ancient plants and sea life.
units.not_here: All three rock types and the rock cycle are T2.
units.lane_note: Teach the process; named places and landforms are the geography bank's.

units.title: Using and Protecting Earth's Resources
units.scope: Natural resources people take from Earth: water, air, soil, rocks and minerals, forests, fuels; renewable resources are replaced by nature in a human lifetime (sunlight, wind, trees, water) and nonrenewable ones are not (coal, oil, natural gas, most minerals); reduce, reuse and recycle; conservation means using less; litter and pollution harm land, water and air.
units.lane_note: Science only: prices and laws are the economics and history banks'.

units.title: Weather and Climate
units.scope: Weather is the state of the air at a place and time: temperature, precipitation, wind, clouds, humidity; climate is a place's usual weather over many years (a desert's climate is dry even on a rainy day); the tools: a thermometer (temperature), a rain gauge (rainfall), a wind vane (wind direction), an anemometer (wind speed), a barometer (air pressure); clouds are made of tiny drops of water or ice, and the main kinds: puffy cumulus, flat grey stratus, thin wispy cirrus high up; the Sun's heat and the ocean drive the weather.
units.not_here: Fronts, air masses and what drives climate are T4.
units.lane_note: Teach the process; named places and landforms are the geography bank's.

units.title: Measuring and the Fair Test
units.scope: The tools of a 5th-grade scientist and what each measures: a metric ruler or metre stick (length, in centimetres and metres), a balance (mass, in grams), a graduated cylinder (volume, in millilitres), a Celsius thermometer (temperature), a spring scale (force), a timer, a hand lens and a microscope (seeing small things). The fair test: ask a testable question, change only one thing and keep everything else the same, measure the result, repeat the trials, record data in a table or graph; a prediction is tested, not just believed.

units.title: Particles in Solids, Liquids and Gases
units.scope: Why the states behave as they do, in particles: in a solid the particles are packed tight and only vibrate in place (fixed shape and volume); in a liquid they are close but slide past one another (fixed volume, no fixed shape); in a gas they are far apart and move fast and freely (fills any container, easy to squeeze); heating gives particles more energy and speed, so solids melt and liquids boil; a gas can be compressed because of the space between its particles.

units.title: Pure Substances and Mixtures
units.scope: A pure substance is an element or a compound with fixed properties (pure water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level); a homogeneous mixture is the same throughout (salt water, air, brass); a heterogeneous mixture has parts that can be seen (granite, sand in water, soil); physical properties (boiling point, density, magnetism, solubility, particle size) are used to tell substances apart and to separate mixtures (filtering, evaporation, magnets, distillation).
units.lane_note: Use lab, rock, nature and body examples, not kitchen or cooking ones (the cooking bank owns those).

units.title: Metals, Nonmetals and Metalloids
units.scope: Elements are listed on the periodic table, each with a one- or two-letter symbol (O oxygen, C carbon, H hydrogen, Fe iron from Latin ferrum, Au gold from aurum, Na sodium, Ag silver). Most elements are metals (shiny, can be hammered into sheets and drawn into wire, conduct heat and electricity), found on the left and in the middle; nonmetals on the right (dull, brittle as solids, poor conductors; many are gases); metalloids such as silicon along the staircase line have some properties of each, which is why silicon is used in computer chips.
units.lane_note: Who mines or trades elements is the economics or history bank's.

units.title: Density: Why Things Float or Sink
units.scope: Density is how much mass is packed into a given volume. An object floats in a liquid that is denser than it and sinks in one that is less dense; liquids of different densities form layers (oil floats on water); ice floats because it is less dense than liquid water; an egg or a swimmer floats more easily in salt water than in fresh water; a large ship floats because its hull holds a lot of air, making the ship as a whole less dense than water.
units.lane_note: Use lab, rock, nature and body examples, not kitchen or cooking ones (the cooking bank owns those).

units.title: Signs of a Chemical Change
units.scope: When substances react and a new substance forms, the evidence can include: a gas given off (bubbles without boiling), a change in temperature on its own (getting hot or cold), a solid forming in a liquid (a precipitate), a colour change, light given off, or a new smell. Examples: iron rusting, wood burning, a glow stick, an antacid tablet fizzing in water, a copper roof turning green. These signs are evidence, not proof: boiling water also bubbles, but no new substance forms.
units.lane_note: Use lab, rock, nature and body examples, not kitchen or cooking ones (the cooking bank owns those).

units.title: Forces and Net Force
units.scope: Kinds of force: gravity, friction, magnetism, applied forces (a push or pull) and the normal force (a surface pushing back up, as a table holds up a book). Forces have a size and a direction; forces on one object add up to a net force; when forces are balanced (net force zero) motion does not change; when unbalanced, the object speeds up, slows down or changes direction; a force diagram uses arrows.
units.lane_note: Arithmetic of net force is the math bank's; ask which way and what happens.

units.title: Action and Reaction: Newton's Third Law
units.scope: For every force there is an equal and opposite force: when one object pushes or pulls another, the second pushes or pulls back just as hard in the opposite direction at the same moment. Examples: a swimmer pushes water back and moves forward; a rocket pushes gas out of its engine and the gas pushes the rocket up; a balloon let go flies around the room; a skater pushing a wall rolls backward. The two forces act on different objects, so they do not cancel.

units.title: Kinetic and Potential Energy
units.scope: Kinetic energy is the energy of motion (faster and heavier means more); potential energy is stored energy: gravitational (because of height), elastic (a stretched rubber band, a drawn bow, a squeezed spring) and chemical (food, fuel, batteries). Energy is never created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another or passed on: a roller coaster trades height for speed and back; a pendulum swings; friction turns some motion into heat.

units.title: Waves Carry Energy
units.scope: A wave carries energy from place to place without carrying the matter along (a floating ball bobs up and down as a wave passes). Transverse waves move the medium at right angles to the wave (a wave sent along a rope; light); longitudinal (compression) waves move it back and forth along the wave's direction (sound, a pushed spring toy). Crest and trough; compression and rarefaction; sound needs a medium (it cannot travel through empty space), light does not.
units.not_here: Amplitude, frequency and the spectrum are T4.

units.title: Cells: The Building Blocks of Life
units.scope: Cell theory: all living things are made of one or more cells; the cell is the basic unit of life; new cells come from cells that already exist. Most cells are too small to see without a microscope; Robert Hooke named cells after the little rooms he saw in cork. One-celled (unicellular) and many-celled (multicellular) living things. Parts and jobs: the cell membrane controls what goes in and out; the nucleus holds the cell's genetic instructions and directs its work; cytoplasm; mitochondria release energy from food; chloroplasts make food from sunlight (plants and algae); the cell wall gives plant cells a stiff outer layer; plant cells have a large central vacuole that stores water. How plant and animal cells differ. Cells without a nucleus (prokaryotes such as bacteria) and with one (eukaryotes). Levels of organisation: cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism.
units.not_here: Cell division, DNA's structure and genetics are later units.

units.title: One Cell or Many
units.scope: Unicellular organisms are a single cell that does everything (bacteria, amoebas, paramecia, many algae, yeast); multicellular organisms are made of many cells that specialise (nerve cells, muscle cells, red blood cells each with a job); autotrophs make their own food (plants, algae) while heterotrophs take it in (animals, fungi); fungi are not plants: they cannot make food and they absorb it; how a paramecium moves (tiny hairs called cilia) and how an amoeba eats (it surrounds food).
units.not_here: The cell's parts are in the pilot unit; do not repeat them.

units.title: Variation and Survival
units.scope: Members of one species differ from one another (size, colour, speed, resistance to disease, tolerance of heat, cold or drought); these differences are variations; when the environment changes (a drought, a cold winter, a new disease), individuals with some variations survive and have young more often than others; variation within a population is why a species can survive a change. Most variation is inherited.
units.not_here: Natural selection by name is T3.
units.lane_note: Teach the general science; one named animal's own anatomy or behaviour is the animal bank's.

units.title: Competing for Resources
units.scope: Living things need resources: food, water, light, space, shelter, mates; when a resource is scarce, organisms compete for it; a limiting factor (the scarcest resource, such as water in a desert or light on a forest floor) sets how large a population can grow; carrying capacity is the largest population an area can support; plants compete for light, water and soil nutrients too.
units.lane_note: Teach the general science; one named animal's own anatomy or behaviour is the animal bank's.

units.title: Predators, Partners and Parasites
units.scope: How species interact: predation (a predator hunts and eats its prey; predator and prey numbers rise and fall together); competition; symbiosis, two species living closely together, in three forms: mutualism (both benefit: bees and flowers, the bacteria in a human gut), commensalism (one benefits and the other is not affected), parasitism (one benefits and its host is harmed: a tick, a tapeworm, mistletoe).
units.lane_note: Use the three kinds as the science; famous partner pairs told for the creature's sake are the animal bank's.

units.title: Populations, Communities and Ecosystems
units.scope: Levels of ecological organisation: an organism is one living thing; a population is all the members of one species in one area; a community is all the populations living together in an area; an ecosystem is the community plus its nonliving surroundings; the biosphere is all of Earth's ecosystems; examples from a pond and a forest.

units.title: The Body's Defences Against Germs
units.scope: How the body keeps out and fights germs: skin as the first barrier; mucus and tiny hairs in the nose and airways trap germs; stomach acid kills many swallowed germs; white blood cells attack germs that get in; a fever slows some germs and speeds the defences; the lymph nodes (glands that swell in the neck) are where white blood cells gather; the body remembers a germ it has beaten and fights it faster next time; washing hands removes germs.
units.not_here: Vaccines are not in this unit (they are a T5 unit).
units.framing_note: Settled immunology, told plainly. No vaccine content.

units.title: Why We Have Seasons
units.scope: Earth's axis is tilted (about 23.5 degrees) and stays pointing the same way in space as Earth orbits the Sun, so for part of the year each hemisphere leans toward the Sun (more direct sunlight, longer days: summer) and for part it leans away (slanting light, shorter days: winter); when it is summer in the Northern Hemisphere it is winter in the Southern; seasons are NOT caused by Earth being closer to the Sun (Earth is actually closest in early January); the solstices (longest and shortest days) and equinoxes (day and night about equal).

units.title: The Tides
units.scope: The Moon's gravity pulls on Earth's oceans and raises a bulge of water; most coasts get two high tides and two low tides about every day (roughly every 12 hours and 25 minutes); the Sun's gravity also affects tides, but less, because it is so much farther away; spring tides (the biggest range) come when the Sun, Moon and Earth line up at new and full moon; neap tides (the smallest range) when they form a right angle at the quarter moons.
units.lane_note: Teach the process; named places and landforms are the geography bank's.

units.title: Moon Phases and Eclipses
units.scope: The Moon shines by reflected sunlight; one half is always lit; as the Moon orbits Earth (about once a month) we see different amounts of the lit half: new moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full moon, then waning back; phases are not caused by Earth's shadow; the same side of the Moon always faces Earth; a solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth (only at new moon); a lunar eclipse when Earth's shadow falls on the Moon (only at full moon).

units.title: Earth's Four Spheres
units.scope: Earth's systems: the geosphere (rock, soil and Earth's interior), the hydrosphere (all water: oceans, rivers, lakes, ice, groundwater, vapour), the atmosphere (the layer of gases around Earth: mostly nitrogen, then oxygen) and the biosphere (all living things); how they act on one another: rain wears down rock, plant roots break rock and plants add oxygen to the air, a volcano adds gases and ash, the ocean warms the air.

units.title: Earth's Layers
units.scope: Earth's layers from the outside in: the crust (thin, solid rock; thicker under continents, thinner under oceans), the mantle (the thickest layer, hot rock that flows very slowly), the outer core (liquid iron and nickel) and the inner core (solid iron and nickel, the hottest part, kept solid by enormous pressure); temperature and pressure rise with depth; the deepest holes ever drilled reach only a few kilometres into the crust.
units.not_here: How we know (seismic waves) is T5.

units.title: The Rock Cycle
units.scope: The three kinds of rock and how each forms: igneous rock when melted rock (magma underground, lava at the surface) cools and hardens (granite cools slowly underground and has large crystals; basalt and glassy obsidian cool fast at the surface); sedimentary rock from layers of sediment pressed and cemented together (sandstone, shale, limestone); metamorphic rock when heat and pressure change an existing rock without melting it (limestone becomes marble, shale becomes slate); any rock can become any other kind over time.
units.lane_note: Teach the process; named places and landforms are the geography bank's.

units.title: Caring for Air, Water and Soil
units.scope: Why managing resources matters (clean air and water, enough food and energy); sources of air pollution (burning fuels, smoke) and water pollution (sewage, fertiliser run-off, oil); soil erosion and how plant cover and terracing stop it; conservation and efficiency (an LED bulb uses far less electricity than an old incandescent bulb for the same light); new technology for cleaner water (filters, treatment plants).
units.lane_note: Science of pollution, efficiency and conservation only; prices, trade-offs and policy are the economics bank's.

units.title: Hypothesis, Theory and Law
units.scope: A hypothesis is a testable idea or prediction ('if... then...'); a scientific theory is a well-tested explanation backed by a large body of evidence (cell theory, plate tectonics), not a guess; a scientific law describes a pattern that always happens, often as a rule or equation (Newton's laws of motion), without explaining why; theories and laws are both strong and do different jobs; an idea that cannot be tested is not a scientific hypothesis.

units.title: Measuring Like a Scientist
units.scope: The metric (SI) units scientists everywhere use: metre (length), kilogram and gram (mass), litre (volume), second (time), degree Celsius (temperature); prefixes kilo- (a thousand), centi- (a hundredth), milli- (a thousandth); quantitative data are numbers, qualitative data are descriptions; why trials are repeated (one result could be a fluke); why the spread of results matters; sources of error (a misread scale, a leaky container).
units.lane_note: Computing an average is the math bank's; ask why scientists repeat and what the spread shows.

units.title: The Microscope and Cell Theory
units.scope: How cell theory was built with the microscope: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek's tiny handmade lenses and the living 'animalcules' he saw in pond water and scraped from teeth; Robert Hooke's microscope and the word 'cell'; Matthias Schleiden (all plants are made of cells) and Theodor Schwann (all animals too); Rudolf Virchow (every cell comes from a cell); how better tools changed what scientists could know; the parts of a light microscope and what each does.
units.not_here: Hooke's cork is already asked in the pilot cells unit; key different facts.

units.title: Elements, Compounds and Formulas
units.scope: An element is made of one kind of atom; a compound is two or more elements chemically joined in fixed proportions, with properties unlike its elements (sodium is a soft metal that reacts violently with water and chlorine is a poisonous gas, yet together they make table salt); molecules; reading a chemical formula: H2O is two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom, CO2 one carbon and two oxygen, NaCl sodium and chlorine; applying it to a new formula (how many atoms of each).
units.lane_note: Use lab, rock, nature and body examples, not kitchen or cooking ones (the cooking bank owns those).

units.title: Physical or Chemical Change
units.scope: Applying the difference: a physical change alters size, shape or state but not the substance (cutting, crushing, breaking glass, melting, freezing, dissolving, boiling); a chemical change makes a new substance with new properties (rusting, burning, tarnishing silver, a firework); classifying new cases and explaining why; why dissolving salt is physical (the salt can be got back by evaporation) and burning a match is chemical.
units.lane_note: Use lab, rock, nature and body examples, not kitchen or cooking ones (the cooking bank owns those).

units.title: Solutions: Solute and Solvent
units.scope: The solute is what dissolves and the solvent what it dissolves in; water dissolves so many substances it is called the universal solvent; concentration (how much solute in a given amount of solution) and dilution (adding more solvent); a solid dissolves faster when the solvent is warmer, when the solid is crushed (more surface area) and when it is stirred or shaken; a saturated solution can hold no more solute; salt in sea water, oxygen dissolved in a pond, carbon dioxide in fizzy water.
units.lane_note: Use lab, rock, nature and body examples, not kitchen or cooking ones (the cooking bank owns those).

units.title: Speed, Velocity and Motion Graphs
units.scope: Average speed is the total distance divided by the total time (kilometres per hour, metres per second); velocity is speed with a direction; reading a distance-time graph: a steeper line means faster, a flat line means stopped, a straight sloped line means steady speed; acceleration as any change in speed or direction (a car turning a corner at steady speed is accelerating); applying these to described trips.
units.lane_note: Keep the arithmetic easy enough to do in the head; the question is what the numbers and slopes mean.

units.title: Inertia: Newton's First Law
units.scope: Newton's first law: an object at rest stays at rest, and a moving object keeps moving in a straight line at the same speed, unless an unbalanced force acts on it; inertia is this resistance to a change in motion, and more mass means more inertia; why passengers lurch forward when a car brakes and why seat belts are needed; why a ball rolling on grass stops (friction); the tablecloth pulled from under the dishes; a spacecraft coasting with its engines off.

units.title: Heat on the Move
units.scope: Thermal energy moves from warmer to cooler things until they reach the same temperature. Conduction: by direct contact (a metal spoon in hot water, a pan handle, a cold metal bench feeling colder than a wooden one); convection: by a moving fluid (warm air rising, sea breezes, a pot of boiling water, currents in the mantle and the ocean); radiation: by electromagnetic waves, even through empty space (sunlight warming Earth, the warmth of a campfire); insulators slow heat flow (air pockets in a coat, foam, a vacuum flask). Applying the three to new cases.

units.title: Temperature and Moving Particles
units.scope: Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of a substance's particles (hotter means faster-moving particles); thermal energy is the total energy of all the particles, so a bathtub of warm water holds more thermal energy than a cup of boiling water; heating makes particles move faster and spread out (thermal expansion: gaps in bridges and railway tracks, a thermometer's liquid rising); cooling slows them; adding or removing energy can change the state; absolute zero as the coldest possible temperature.

units.title: Mendel's Peas and Inherited Traits
units.scope: Traits are passed from parents to offspring (inherited traits) as opposed to traits gained in life (acquired or learned). Gregor Mendel, a monk, bred pea plants in his monastery garden and tracked clear traits such as tall and short stems. Crossing pure tall with pure short gave a first generation that was all tall; the short trait came back in about one in four plants of the next generation (about 3 to 1). Dominant and recessive traits; a recessive trait shows only when an offspring gets it from both parents. Each parent passes on one of its two copies of a gene (alleles). Punnett squares predict the chances of a trait. Genotype and phenotype as words for the gene pair and the trait that shows. Mendel's work was overlooked until about 1900. Applying the ideas to a new cross (predict the share of offspring with a trait).
units.not_here: DNA's structure, meiosis in detail, and natural selection are other units.

units.title: Energy Through the Food Web
units.scope: Trophic levels: producers, primary consumers (herbivores), secondary and tertiary consumers; an energy pyramid shows the energy available shrinking at each level up, because most of the energy is used for living or lost as heat (roughly a tenth passes on, a rule of thumb); why there are far fewer top predators than plants; why a food chain rarely has more than four or five links; matter cycles while energy flows through.
units.lane_note: Teach the general science; one named animal's own anatomy or behaviour is the animal bank's.

units.title: Body Systems: Heart, Lungs, Gut and Kidneys
units.scope: How the supply systems work together: the circulatory system (the heart's four chambers, arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins back, capillaries where exchange happens, red blood cells carry oxygen); the respiratory system (air down the windpipe to the lungs' tiny air sacs, oxygen into the blood, carbon dioxide out); the digestive system (mouth, stomach, small intestine where most nutrients are absorbed, large intestine where water is taken back); the urinary system (kidneys filter waste from the blood); cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form systems.
units.not_here: The body's defences against germs are a T2 unit.

units.title: Body Systems: Bones, Muscles, Nerves and Glands
units.scope: The skeletal system supports, protects and makes blood cells in the marrow (an adult has 206 bones); muscles work in pairs and pull, never push (biceps and triceps); the nervous system: the brain, the spinal cord and nerves, senses sending signals to the brain, a reflex that skips the brain; the endocrine system's glands release hormones into the blood: the pituitary (growth), the thyroid (how fast the body uses food), the pancreas (insulin; too little causes diabetes), the adrenal glands (adrenaline in fright); the skin as an organ.
units.lane_note: Clinical and brief; nothing about the reproductive system beyond its name.

units.title: Two Ways to Make Offspring
units.scope: Asexual reproduction needs one parent and makes offspring identical to it, quickly (bacteria splitting in two, yeast budding, mould spores, strawberry runners, potato eyes, a planarian regrowing); sexual reproduction joins cells from two parents and makes varied offspring, which helps a population survive change; a flower's parts: petals attract pollinators, the stamen makes pollen, the pistil holds the ovary where seeds form; pollination by wind, insects and birds; the ovary ripens into a fruit.
units.lane_note: Plant- and microbe-led; animal reproduction only as the general idea, clinical and brief.

units.title: Natural and Artificial Selection
units.scope: Natural selection: individuals whose inherited traits suit their environment survive and reproduce more, so those traits become more common over generations (Charles Darwin's idea); it acts on populations over generations, not on one animal in its lifetime; artificial selection: people choose which plants and animals breed (wild mustard bred into cabbage, broccoli and kale; wolves into dog breeds; wild grass into corn); applying the idea to a new case (bacteria resisting an antibiotic, insects resisting a pesticide).
units.lane_note: Teach the general science; one named animal's own anatomy or behaviour is the animal bank's.

units.title: Classifying Living Things
units.scope: Carl Linnaeus and the system scientists use: the ranks kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species; the two-part scientific name (genus and species, as in Homo sapiens) so scientists everywhere mean the same organism; why common names mislead (a jellyfish is not a fish, a starfish is not a fish); the kingdoms and domains; how scientists use shared features, and now DNA, to group living things; a dichotomous key sorts organisms by yes-or-no choices.
units.lane_note: Teach the general science; one named animal's own anatomy or behaviour is the animal bank's.

units.title: Comets, Asteroids and Moons
units.scope: Beyond the eight planets: moons (Jupiter and Saturn have dozens); the gas giants (Jupiter, Saturn) and the ice giants (Uranus, Neptune); asteroids, rocky bodies mostly in the belt between Mars and Jupiter; comets, icy bodies whose tails point away from the Sun; a meteoroid is a space rock, a meteor the streak of light ('shooting star') as it burns in the air, a meteorite the piece that reaches the ground; the Kuiper belt beyond Neptune (home of Pluto) and the far Oort cloud.
units.not_here: The basic planet facts are T1; key new facts here.

units.title: Gravity and Orbits
units.scope: Gravity pulls every mass toward every other mass; the pull is stronger for bigger masses and weaker with distance; the Sun's gravity holds the planets in orbit and the planets hold their moons; an orbit is forward motion continually bent by gravity (a ball thrown fast enough would fall around the Earth); weight is the pull of gravity and changes from planet to planet while mass stays the same; astronauts in orbit float because they are falling around Earth with their spacecraft, not because there is no gravity.

units.title: Why Earth Can Support Life
units.scope: What makes Earth habitable: its distance from the Sun lets water stay liquid (the habitable or Goldilocks zone); plenty of water; an atmosphere with oxygen to breathe; the ozone layer blocking much of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet light; enough greenhouse warming to keep temperatures mild; a magnetic field that shields from the solar wind; compared with Venus (a runaway greenhouse, far too hot) and Mars (thin air, too cold, little liquid water).

units.title: Plates at Work
units.scope: Earth's crust and upper mantle are broken into plates that move a few centimetres a year, carried by slow heat-driven currents in the mantle; at divergent boundaries plates move apart (mid-ocean ridges, new sea floor); at convergent boundaries they collide (mountain ranges) or one dives under the other (deep trenches, chains of volcanoes); at transform boundaries they slide past (earthquakes along faults); hot spots make chains of volcanic islands as a plate moves over them; most earthquakes and volcanoes happen near plate boundaries.
units.lane_note: Teach the process; named places and landforms are the geography bank's.

units.title: Fossils, Layers and a Changing Earth
units.scope: Evidence that Earth has changed: fossils of sea creatures high in mountains; fossils of the same land plants and reptiles on continents now separated by oceans (the seed fern Glossopteris across the southern continents); coal (from swamp forests) found in Antarctica; superposition: in undisturbed layers the oldest rock lies at the bottom; layers bent or broken after they formed; matching rock types and mountain belts across oceans.
units.not_here: Wegener's story is the T3 method unit; key the evidence here.
units.lane_note: Teach the process; named places and landforms are the geography bank's.

units.title: Watersheds and Groundwater
units.scope: A watershed is all the land that drains into one river, lake or bay; whatever falls on it (rain, fertiliser, oil) can end up downstream; surface water vs groundwater; an aquifer is underground rock or sediment that holds water in its pores and cracks; the water table; wells; how paving, farming, dams and pollution change the water; people depend on the ocean and change it (overfishing, plastics).
units.lane_note: Teach the process; named places and landforms are the geography bank's.

units.title: Designing a Controlled Experiment
units.scope: The independent variable is what the experimenter changes, the dependent variable what is measured, controlled variables what is kept the same; a control group gets no treatment, to compare against; why only one variable is changed at a time; why many trials and a large sample are needed; reading a described experiment and naming its variables, spotting a flaw (two things changed at once), saying what a result shows.

units.title: Redi's Jars and Life from Life
units.scope: The old idea of spontaneous generation (that maggots come from rotting meat, mice from grain); Francesco Redi's experiment of 1668: meat in open jars got maggots, meat in sealed jars did not, and meat under gauze got none on the meat though flies laid eggs on the gauze; why the gauze jar mattered (air could still reach the meat); maggots hatch from flies' eggs; what a control is for; later doubters and the microscope's tiny organisms keeping the question open until Pasteur.
units.not_here: Pasteur's swan-neck flasks are in the T5 germ unit; mention him only in passing.

units.title: Reading Deep Time
units.scope: How geologists read Earth's history in rock: the law of superposition (lower layers are older, Nicolas Steno); relative age (which is older) vs absolute age in years; index fossils that date layers in different places; the geologic time scale (eons, eras, periods) built from rock layers and fossils; Earth is about 4.6 billion years old; if Earth's history were one day, humans arrive in the last few seconds.

units.title: Wegener and the Drifting Continents
units.scope: Alfred Wegener's continental drift (1912): the jigsaw fit of South America and Africa, matching fossils and rocks across oceans, coal in Antarctica; Pangaea; why most geologists rejected it (no known force could push continents through solid rock); decades later, mapping the sea floor (Marie Tharp's maps of the mid-ocean ridges, the magnetic stripes in the sea floor) supplied the evidence, and plate tectonics became accepted; science changes when new evidence arrives.
units.lane_note: Geography has a "how we know the map moves" ladder: key the ridicule, the missing mechanism and the sea-floor vindication.
units.framing_note: Dissent honoured at a 7th-grader's level: the outsider was right about the movement and wrong about the mechanism; the evidence decided.

units.title: Inside the Atom
units.scope: Atoms are made of protons (positive charge), neutrons (no charge) and electrons (negative charge). Protons and neutrons sit in the tiny nucleus, which holds almost all of the atom's mass; electrons move in a cloud around it, and the atom is mostly empty space. The number of protons (the atomic number) decides which element an atom is. In a neutral atom the electrons equal the protons. The outermost (valence) electrons decide how an atom reacts. The experiments that found this: J. J. Thomson's cathode-ray tube and the electron (and his plum-pudding model); Ernest Rutherford's gold-foil experiment, in which most alpha particles passed straight through but a few bounced back, showing a small, dense, positive nucleus; Niels Bohr's electrons in energy levels; James Chadwick's discovery of the neutron.
units.not_here: Chemical bonding, the full periodic table and nuclear reactions are other units.

units.title: Chemical Reactions Conserve Mass
units.scope: In a chemical reaction the atoms of the reactants rearrange into products; no atom is made or destroyed, so the total mass stays the same (Antoine Lavoisier's careful weighing in sealed vessels); when a gas escapes an open container the mass seems to drop; burning a log leaves less ash because most of it goes into the air as gas; counting atoms on each side of a balanced equation; what the arrow and the numbers in front mean.
units.lane_note: Use lab, rock, nature and body examples, not kitchen or cooking ones (the cooking bank owns those).

units.title: Water's Sticky Properties
units.scope: Why water behaves as it does: a water molecule has a slightly negative end (oxygen) and slightly positive ends (hydrogens), so molecules cling together; cohesion (water beads into drops), adhesion (water clings to other surfaces and climbs narrow tubes), surface tension (a 'skin' that holds up a carefully laid paper clip; soap breaks it); together they help pull water up the thin tubes of a plant; why ice floats (its molecules lock into an open pattern).
units.lane_note: Teach the general science; one named animal's own anatomy or behaviour is the animal bank's.

units.title: Acids, Bases and pH
units.scope: The pH scale runs from 0 to 14; pure water is neutral at 7; acids are below 7 (stomach acid, battery acid, acid rain), bases above 7 (soap, ammonia, bleach, antacid); each step on the scale is ten times stronger; indicators change colour to show acid or base (litmus paper turns red in acid and blue in base; red cabbage juice is a home-made indicator); an acid and a base neutralise each other (an antacid tablet for heartburn).
units.lane_note: Use lab, rock, nature and body examples, not kitchen or cooking ones (the cooking bank owns those). Red cabbage juice as an indicator is fine as a test-it-yourself experiment.

units.title: Newton's Laws: Force, Mass and Acceleration
units.scope: Newton's second law: acceleration depends on the net force and the mass (force = mass x acceleration; force measured in newtons); the same push accelerates a light cart more than a heavy one; a bigger force gives a bigger acceleration; the three laws working together: seat belts and air bags (inertia), a rocket launch (action and reaction), a soccer kick, a catch, a tackle; Isaac Newton set out the three laws in his Principia (1687).
units.lane_note: Calculations are the math bank's; ask how force, mass and acceleration trade off.

units.title: Amplitude, Wavelength and Frequency
units.scope: Describing a wave: amplitude (its height; the energy it carries, heard as loudness), wavelength (crest to crest), frequency (waves per second, in hertz; heard as pitch, seen as colour); higher frequency means shorter wavelength; sound needs a medium and travels about 343 metres a second in air, faster in water and steel; light travels about 300,000 kilometres a second and needs no medium; counting the seconds between lightning and thunder to judge distance.

units.title: The Electromagnetic Spectrum
units.scope: Light is one small band of a family of waves that all travel at the speed of light: radio, microwaves, infrared, visible light (red to violet), ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays, from long wavelength to short; their uses (radio and phones, microwave ovens, TV remotes and night cameras, sterilising with UV, X-rays of bones, gamma rays against cancer); how the invisible bands were found: William Herschel's thermometer warming past the red end of a spectrum (infrared, 1800), Johann Ritter's silver chloride darkening past the violet (ultraviolet), Wilhelm Roentgen's X-ray of his wife's hand.

units.title: Fields: Pushes and Pulls Without Touching
units.scope: Forces that act at a distance through fields: gravity, electric and magnetic forces; like charges repel and unlike attract (a balloon rubbed on hair sticks to a wall); like magnetic poles repel, unlike attract; Earth is a giant magnet (a compass needle points north); the forces grow with more charge or a stronger magnet and weaken with distance; an electric current in a coil of wire makes an electromagnet (Hans Christian Oersted's compass needle twitching beside a wire, 1820).

units.title: Genes, Chromosomes and Mutations
units.scope: Genes are sections of DNA carried on chromosomes in the nucleus; humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes, one set from each parent; a gene holds instructions for a trait; an offspring gets half its genes from each parent, which is why siblings differ; a mutation is a change in a gene: harmful (sickle-cell disease from a single change), helpful, or neither; mutations are a source of new variation; X and Y chromosomes decide biological sex in humans (XX female, XY male).
units.not_here: Mendel's crosses and Punnett squares are T3; DNA's structure and protein-making are T5.

units.title: Three Kinds of Adaptation
units.scope: Adaptations grow out of inherited variation over many generations: structural (body parts, colouring, camouflage, mimicry), behavioural (migration, hibernation, hunting in groups) and physiological (control of body temperature, venom, antifreeze proteins in polar fish); sorting new examples into the three kinds; why an adaptation that helps in one environment can hurt in another.
units.lane_note: Teach the general science; one named animal's own anatomy or behaviour is the animal bank's.

units.title: When a Food Web Breaks
units.scope: How a change ripples through a food web: removing a top predator lets its prey multiply and overeat their food (a trophic cascade, as when wolves returned to Yellowstone and elk browsing on riverside trees fell); invasive species with no natural predators (cane toads, rabbits in Australia, zebra mussels); a population boom or crash; a fire, flood or drought; pesticides building up through a food chain (DDT thinning eagles' eggshells).
units.lane_note: A named park or country may set the scene; the ecology is the point. Not one creature's biology for its own sake.

units.title: Ecological Succession
units.scope: Ecological succession: the gradual change of the species in a place over time; primary succession starts on bare rock with no soil (cooled lava, ground left by a melting glacier) with pioneer species such as lichens and mosses that slowly make soil, then grasses, shrubs and trees; secondary succession follows a disturbance that leaves the soil (a forest fire, an abandoned farm field) and goes faster; a climax community; how diversity grows along the way.
units.lane_note: Teach the process; named places and landforms are the geography bank's.

units.title: Biodiversity and Stability
units.scope: Biodiversity is the variety of species and of genes in a place; an ecosystem with many species withstands and recovers from change better (if one food source fails, others remain); ecosystem services (clean water, pollination, fertile soil, flood control); losing biodiversity weakens ecosystems; a field planted with one crop (a monoculture) is easier for one pest or disease to wipe out, as in Ireland's potato famine.
units.lane_note: The ecology, not the history or the economics of the famine.

units.title: Photosynthesis: Atoms In and Out
units.scope: Photosynthesis as a chemical reaction: six carbon dioxide molecules and six water molecules, with light energy, become one glucose molecule and six oxygen molecules; it happens in the chloroplasts; the oxygen comes from the water; the carbon in a tree's wood comes from the air; Jan van Helmont's willow tree gained many kilograms while its soil lost only a few grams, and Joseph Priestley's mint plant kept the air in a sealed jar fit for a mouse (the first clues); light energy stored as chemical energy.
units.not_here: Cellular respiration and enzymes are T5.

units.title: Clues to Common Ancestry
units.scope: Evidence that living things share ancestors: the fossil record's order (simple forms in older rock, more complex ones later); transitional fossils (Tiktaalik, a fish with limb-like fins; Archaeopteryx, with feathers and teeth; early whales with legs); homologous structures (the same bones in a human arm, a bat's wing, a whale's flipper and a cat's leg); similar early embryos; vestigial structures (a whale's tiny hip bones).
units.lane_note: Homology as evidence, not one animal's anatomy for its own sake.

units.title: The Life Cycles of Stars
units.scope: Stars form in clouds of gas and dust (nebulae) pulled together by gravity; a star's mass decides its life: a Sun-like star shines for about ten billion years, swells into a red giant and ends as a white dwarf; a massive star burns faster, becomes a red supergiant and explodes as a supernova, leaving a neutron star or a black hole; star colour shows temperature (red stars are cooler, blue stars hotter); the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram plots brightness against temperature, and most stars, the Sun among them, lie on the main sequence.

units.title: Galaxies and the Expanding Universe
units.scope: Galaxies are vast systems of billions of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity: spiral, elliptical and irregular; the solar system is in a spiral arm of the Milky Way, far from its centre; a light-year is the distance light travels in a year; Henrietta Leavitt's pulsing stars that measure distance; Edwin Hubble showed the Andromeda 'nebula' is a separate galaxy and that distant galaxies are moving away (their light shifted to red); the universe is expanding from a hot, dense beginning about 13.8 billion years ago (the Big Bang); the cosmic microwave background as its leftover glow.
units.not_here: How spectra reveal composition is T5.

units.title: Winds, Air Masses and Fronts
units.scope: Weather is the state of the air day to day; climate the long-run pattern of a place; the Sun heats Earth unevenly (strongly at the equator, weakly at the poles), and air flows from high pressure to low pressure as wind; Earth's spin bends winds (the Coriolis effect) into belts: trade winds, westerlies, polar easterlies; jet streams steer storms; air masses (warm or cold, moist or dry) meet at fronts: a cold front brings short, sharp storms, a warm front longer, gentler rain; a barometer measures air pressure and falling pressure warns of a storm; ocean currents carry heat.
units.lane_note: Teach the process; named places and landforms are the geography bank's.

units.title: How Hurricanes Form
units.scope: Tropical cyclones form over warm ocean water (about 26 degrees Celsius or warmer): warm, moist air rises, its water vapour condenses and releases heat that powers the storm, and Earth's spin sets it turning; called hurricanes in the Atlantic and eastern Pacific, typhoons in the western Pacific; the calm eye, the eyewall with the strongest winds, the spiral rain bands; storm surge is often the deadliest part; a hurricane weakens over land or cold water because it loses its fuel; they spin counter-clockwise north of the equator and clockwise south of it.
units.lane_note: How storms form; named storms and their human stories are history and geography's.

units.title: The Greenhouse Effect
units.scope: The physics: sunlight warms Earth's surface, the surface gives off infrared heat, and greenhouse gases (water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane) absorb and re-send some of it, keeping Earth far warmer than it would otherwise be (on average about 33 degrees Celsius warmer); John Tyndall measured gases absorbing heat in 1859; Svante Arrhenius estimated the warming from doubling carbon dioxide in 1896; Charles David Keeling's measurements on Mauna Loa from 1958 show carbon dioxide rising every year; the carbon cycle's stores (air, oceans, living things, rocks and fossil fuels); natural changes too: a large volcanic eruption cools the planet for a year or two (Tambora's 'year without a summer').
units.framing_note: Settled physics stated flatly (moral_vision; config framing). No forecasts, no policy and no alarm here; what drives climate overall, the record and the honest open questions are the T5 climate unit.

units.title: Correlation, Causation and Error
units.scope: Thinking with data: two things rising together (a correlation) need not mean one causes the other (ice-cream sales and drownings both rise in summer because of the heat); a hidden third factor; precision (results close together) vs accuracy (results close to the true value); measurement error; why a bigger sample and more trials help; survivorship bias (Abraham Wald and the bombers that came back); a graph that is linear vs one that is not.
units.lane_note: The statistics themselves are the math bank's; ask what the data can and cannot show.

units.title: Testing a Claim: Blindfolds and Fair Trials
units.scope: How a claim is put to a fair test: Benjamin Franklin's commission of 1784 blindfolded people to test Franz Mesmer's 'animal magnetism' (they felt effects only when they believed they were being treated); Clever Hans, the horse that seemed to count but was reading his trainer's unconscious cues; Emily Rosa, aged nine, testing 'therapeutic touch' practitioners with a screen (they did no better than chance); why blinding matters; the placebo effect; a test announced in advance.
units.framing_note: The Discovery Pattern: test it yourself; skepticism of a claim, even an expert-endorsed one, is the scientist's first virtue. Present, never mock.

units.title: When the Experts Were Wrong
units.scope: Reversals the evidence won: Barry Marshall drank a broth of Helicobacter pylori bacteria to show they cause stomach ulcers (most doctors blamed stress and acid; Nobel Prize 2005); Dan Shechtman's quasicrystals, ridiculed and then awarded a Nobel Prize (2011); Lynn Margulis, rejected by many journals, was right that mitochondria and chloroplasts descend from captured bacteria; J Harlen Bretz's giant Ice Age floods, mocked for forty years; what changed each mind (a test, new evidence), and the honest lesson: consensus is not proof, and an outsider is not always right either.
units.framing_note: STANCE (T4-T5 only, 9th-grade level): dissent honoured. The test, not the authority, settled each case. Steel-man the doubters of the day (they had reasons); no smug voice; no sermon.

units.title: Science's Dark Chapters
units.scope: When science and medicine did harm, and what was learned: the Radium Girls, factory workers poisoned by radium paint they were told was safe, whose lawsuits changed worker safety; thalidomide, a sleeping pill sold in many countries in the late 1950s that caused severe birth defects, and Frances Kelsey, the FDA reviewer who refused to approve it in the United States because the evidence of its safety was not good enough; the Tuskegee study (1932-1972), in which US government doctors watched Black men with syphilis go untreated, even after penicillin became the cure; informed consent as the lesson.
units.lane_note: Teen audience: no graphic detail of injuries.
units.framing_note: STANCE (T4-T5 only, 9th-grade level): the dark chapters as the standing warning, told plainly at a 9th-grade level: name who did it; one clause of harm, no gore; Frances Kelsey's demand for evidence as the heroine. Keep to the science and medicine; the politics and court history are the history bank's.

units.title: Momentum and Collisions
units.scope: Momentum is mass times velocity; a moving truck is harder to stop than a bicycle at the same speed; in a collision with no outside force, total momentum is conserved (a cue ball stopping dead as the struck ball rolls on; a rifle's recoil; a skater pushing off another); impulse: stretching a collision over more time lowers the force (crumple zones, air bags, helmets, bending the knees when landing, a catcher's padded glove).
units.lane_note: Formula work is the math bank's; ask what the trade-off means.

units.title: Fission, Fusion and Mass-Energy
units.scope: The four fundamental forces (gravity, electromagnetism, the strong nuclear force that holds the nucleus together, the weak force behind some radioactive decay); fission splits heavy nuclei such as uranium-235 and releases energy and more neutrons (a chain reaction), as in nuclear power plants; Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch explained fission in 1938-39; fusion joins light nuclei (hydrogen into helium), as in the Sun; E = mc2: a little mass becomes a great deal of energy; nuclear power's benefits and its waste.
units.lane_note: Weapons and their history are the history bank's; no weapon design detail.

units.title: Circuits, Motors and Generators
units.scope: Series circuits (one path: one bulb out, all out) vs parallel circuits (separate branches, as in house wiring); current (the flow of charge, in amperes), voltage (the push, in volts) and resistance (in ohms) in words (Ohm's law); an electric current makes a magnetic field, which is how a motor turns electricity into motion; a changing magnetic field makes a current (electromagnetic induction, Michael Faraday, 1831), which is how a generator turns motion into electricity; a motor and a generator are the same machine run in opposite directions.

units.title: Energy's Two Great Laws
units.scope: The first law: energy is conserved in a closed system, changing form but never created or destroyed (James Joule's paddle wheel warming water showed that work and heat are exchangeable); the second law: heat flows by itself only from hot to cold and energy spreads out, so no machine turns all its energy into useful work and some is always lost as heat (entropy rises); why perpetual-motion machines always fail; Count Rumford boring cannons and the end of the caloric fluid theory; efficiency of real machines.

units.title: Waves at Work
units.scope: Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength; interference: waves add up (constructive) or cancel (destructive), as in noise-cancelling headphones; reflection used in sonar, ultrasound scans and radar; refraction in lenses and fibre optics (light bouncing along a glass thread); the Doppler effect (a siren's pitch drops as it passes; radar guns and weather radar); digital signals are more reliable to store and send than analog ones.

units.title: The Periodic Table's Patterns
units.scope: The periodic table is ordered by atomic number; elements in a column (group) share properties because they have the same number of valence electrons: the alkali metals (very reactive; sodium and potassium react violently with water), the halogens, the noble gases (full outer shells, almost never react); properties change steadily across a row (period); metals on the left, nonmetals on the right; Dmitri Mendeleev left gaps in his 1869 table and predicted elements not yet found (gallium, germanium); Henry Moseley showed the order is really by the number of protons.

units.title: Light from Atoms
units.scope: When an atom's electron is energised it jumps to a higher energy level, and when it drops back it gives off light of an exact colour; each element has its own pattern of colours (an emission spectrum), a fingerprint: firework and flame-test colours (sodium yellow, copper green-blue, strontium red), neon signs; dark lines in sunlight's spectrum (Joseph von Fraunhofer) reveal the elements in stars; helium was found in the Sun's spectrum (1868) before it was found on Earth; Cecilia Payne showed stars are made mostly of hydrogen.

units.title: Balancing Equations and Reaction Rates
units.scope: Balancing a chemical equation so atoms, and so mass, are conserved (hydrogen and oxygen making water: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O); kinds of reaction (combustion, rusting and other oxidation, an acid neutralised by a base, an acid fizzing on a metal); what speeds a reaction: higher temperature, higher concentration, more surface area (a cloud of fine dust can explode while a lump burns slowly), stirring, and a catalyst, which speeds a reaction without being used up (the catalytic converter in a car).
units.lane_note: Use lab, rock, nature and body examples, not kitchen or cooking ones (the cooking bank owns those).

units.title: The Molecules of Life
units.scope: The four kinds of large molecule in living things and their jobs: carbohydrates (sugars and starches for quick energy; cellulose in plant cell walls), lipids (fats and oils for stored energy; the cell membrane), proteins (enzymes, muscle, hair, antibodies; built from amino acids), nucleic acids (DNA and RNA, which carry information); the cell membrane controls what passes by diffusion (from more crowded to less), osmosis (the diffusion of water) and active transport (using energy); why a slug shrivels in salt and a raisin swells in water.
units.lane_note: Nutrition and diets are cooking-adjacent; keep to what the molecules do in cells.

units.title: Viruses, Bacteria and Antibiotics
units.scope: A bacterium is a living single cell; a virus is genetic material in a protein coat that can copy itself only inside a host cell, so most scientists do not count it as alive; viruses are far smaller than bacteria (they passed through filters that caught bacteria); antibiotics kill bacteria or stop them growing but do nothing against viruses (so they cannot cure a cold); Alexander Fleming noticed in 1928 that a mould (Penicillium) had killed the bacteria around it on a dish; antibiotic resistance evolves when the few resistant bacteria survive a treatment and multiply.
units.framing_note: Settled microbiology. No pathogen-enhancement or engineering detail of any kind; vaccines are not in this unit.

units.title: The Cell Cycle
units.scope: A cell's life: interphase (it grows and copies its DNA), mitosis (prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase: the copied chromosomes are pulled apart into two nuclei) and cytokinesis (the cell divides into two identical cells); why the body needs mitosis (growth, repair, replacing cells: red blood cells live about four months); one fertilised egg becomes trillions of specialised cells by differentiation; stem cells; cancer as cell division escaping its controls.

units.title: From DNA to Protein
units.scope: DNA is a double helix of two strands; its four bases pair A with T and C with G; Rosalind Franklin's X-ray image (Photo 51) helped James Watson and Francis Crick work out the structure in 1953; base pairing lets DNA copy itself; a gene's sequence is copied into messenger RNA (transcription) and read at the ribosomes, three bases at a time, to build a protein from amino acids (translation); a mutation can change one amino acid and so a protein (sickle-cell haemoglobin); PCR copies DNA and gel electrophoresis sorts it by size (DNA fingerprinting).

units.title: Meiosis and Patterns of Inheritance
units.scope: Meiosis halves the chromosome number to make egg and sperm cells (23 chromosomes each in humans), and crossing over and independent assortment shuffle genes so siblings differ; patterns beyond simple dominance: incomplete dominance (red and white snapdragons giving pink), codominance (AB blood type), multiple alleles (the A, B and O blood-group alleles), sex-linked traits carried on the X chromosome (red-green colour blindness and haemophilia are more common in males); a two-trait cross.

units.title: How Evolution Works
units.scope: Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace reached natural selection independently (their papers read together in 1858); its conditions: inherited variation, more offspring than can survive, competition, so some variants leave more offspring; populations evolve, individuals do not; speciation when separated populations change until they can no longer interbreed; genetic drift (chance, strongest in small populations), gene flow and mutation; molecular evidence (shared DNA: humans and chimpanzees share most of their DNA); Richard Lenski's bacteria evolving in flasks for tens of thousands of generations; Lamarck's inheritance of acquired traits as the respectable wrong rival.
units.lane_note: Teach the general science; one named animal's own anatomy or behaviour is the animal bank's.

units.title: Respiration and Enzymes
units.scope: Cellular respiration releases the energy stored in glucose, in the mitochondria: glucose and oxygen become carbon dioxide and water, and the energy is stored in a molecule called ATP; it is roughly photosynthesis run in reverse; aerobic respiration (with oxygen) vs anaerobic (without: fermentation, and the lactic acid in tired muscles); enzymes are proteins that speed reactions by lowering the energy needed to start them, each shaped to fit its own substrate (lock and key), and they stop working when heat or the wrong pH changes their shape (a fever too high is dangerous for this reason).
units.lane_note: The cellular process only; fermentation in bread or brewing is the cooking bank's.

units.title: How the Sun Shines
units.scope: In the Sun's core, at about 15 million degrees Celsius, hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium, turning a little mass into a great deal of energy; that energy takes a very long time to work out of the Sun (many thousands of years) but its light then reaches Earth in about eight minutes; the Sun is about 4.6 billion years old and roughly halfway through its life; sunspots, the 11-year cycle, solar flares and space weather; stars forge heavier elements, and supernovae scatter them, so the atoms in living things were made in stars.

units.title: Reading the Big Bang in Light
units.scope: The evidence for the Big Bang: the red shift of distant galaxies (the farther the galaxy, the faster it recedes: Hubble's law); the cosmic microwave background, found by accident in 1964 by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, who at first suspected pigeon droppings in their antenna; the universe's ordinary matter is about three-quarters hydrogen and one-quarter helium, as the theory predicts; the name 'Big Bang' coined by its rival Fred Hoyle; what is still unknown (dark matter and dark energy).
units.framing_note: MYSTERY honoured: what dark matter and dark energy are is still unknown; say so plainly.

units.title: Kepler's Laws and Newton's Gravity
units.scope: Johannes Kepler, using Tycho Brahe's careful observations, found that planets move in ellipses with the Sun at one focus, move fastest when nearest the Sun, and take longer to orbit the farther out they are; Isaac Newton explained all three with universal gravitation: every mass attracts every other, and the pull falls with the square of the distance (twice as far, a quarter of the pull); Neptune was found in 1846 where calculations from Uranus's wobbles said it must be; Henry Cavendish weighed the Earth with a torsion balance.
units.lane_note: Orbital arithmetic is the math bank's.

units.title: Earth's Interior and Age
units.scope: How we know what is inside Earth: earthquake waves bend and change speed as they pass through different layers; S-waves cannot pass through liquid, so their 'shadow' showed the outer core is liquid; Inge Lehmann found the solid inner core in 1936; sea-floor rock is youngest at the mid-ocean ridges and older farther away (sea-floor spreading); radiometric dating uses the steady decay of radioactive atoms (half-life) as a clock; Clair Patterson dated meteorites to about 4.55 billion years in 1956, the age of Earth.

units.title: What Drives Earth's Climate
units.scope: Climate changes when the energy flowing in and out changes: the Sun's output, slow cycles in Earth's orbit and tilt (Milutin Milankovic's calculations of the ice ages), volcanic ash, greenhouse gases; feedbacks (melting ice uncovers darker ground and sea that absorb more sunlight; water vapour); the record shows climate has always changed (ice ages, the warm Eocene, the Medieval Warm Period, the Little Ice Age when the Thames froze); Earth has warmed about 1.1-1.3 degrees Celsius since the late 1800s and carbon dioxide absorbs infrared (settled); how much of the warming is from people and how much harm lies ahead are argued among scientists (Steven Koonin's Unsettled, 2021); forecasts with dates that failed (an ice-free Arctic summer predicted for 2013); satellites measure a greening Earth.
units.framing_note: STANCE (T4-T5 only, 9th-grade level): the config framing on climate: greenhouse physics and the warming stated flatly; the overstatement and the failed dated predictions named and attributed; Koonin's view as a mature scientific one, attributed; no 'denier' and no alarm in the bank's own voice; no policy verdict. Present, never preach; steel-man the mainstream assessment (the IPCC) before the critique.

units.title: How Germs Were Proven
units.scope: How we know that germs cause disease, told as evidence and reasoning. The rival ideas: spontaneous generation (life from non-life) and miasma (disease from bad air). Ignaz Semmelweis in Vienna in 1847: two maternity clinics, the doctors' clinic with a far higher death rate from childbed fever than the midwives'; a colleague died after a scalpel cut during an autopsy; Semmelweis made the doctors wash their hands in chlorinated lime, and deaths fell sharply; his colleagues rejected the idea and he died in an asylum. John Snow's map of the 1854 Broad Street cholera outbreak and the pump handle. Louis Pasteur's swan-neck flasks: air could reach the broth but dust and microbes were trapped in the bend, and the broth stayed clear until the neck was broken (why that design answered the objection that broth needs air). Robert Koch's steps for proving that a particular microbe causes a particular disease. Joseph Lister's carbolic acid in surgery. What a control group is for, and what each experiment ruled out.
units.not_here: Vaccines and modern public-health policy are not in this unit.
units.framing_note: Dissent honoured: Semmelweis was right and the medical consensus of his day was wrong; the test, not the authority, settled it. Tell it plainly, no sermon.

units.title: Fair Trials: Controls, Blinding and Placebos
units.scope: How medicine learned to test: James Lind's 1747 trial on a ship, twelve sailors with scurvy in six pairs given six treatments (only the pair given oranges and lemons recovered quickly); the control group; the placebo effect (a sugar pill can make people feel better); single- and double-blind trials (neither the patient nor the doctor knows who got what) and why; randomisation; the 1954 Francis field trial of the polio vaccine as the largest such test of its day; why one success story is not evidence.

units.title: When Results Do Not Replicate
units.scope: Replication is the test of a finding: John Ioannidis argued in 2005 that most published research findings may be false; in 2015 a large project could reproduce only about 36 of 100 published psychology results; p-hacking (trying analyses until one looks significant) and the file drawer (unexciting results left unpublished); peer review checks a paper's reasoning but is not a truth detector (it missed the fabricated data of Diederik Stapel and Jan Hendrik Schon, both later caught by others); honest reporting and replication as science's self-correction.
units.framing_note: STANCE (T4-T5 only, 9th-grade level): science the method celebrated, the institution covered honestly: the crisis is real and documented; the cure is more and better testing, not less trust in evidence. Attribute every figure.

units.title: Vaccines: The Science and the Scrutiny
units.scope: The immunology (settled): a vaccine shows the immune system a harmless form or part of a germ so it makes antibodies and memory cells; Edward Jenner's cowpox and James Phipps (1796), and the older practice of variolation (Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, Onesimus in Boston); smallpox declared eradicated in 1980. The scrutiny (documented): the 1955 Cutter Incident, when a faulty batch of polio vaccine paralysed and killed children; the 1986 US law that shields vaccine makers from most lawsuits and set up a no-fault compensation court; reporting systems that catch only a fraction of side effects; the US childhood schedule has grown from a handful of shots to dozens of doses; informed consent as the rule (the Nuremberg Code); critics such as Robert F. Kennedy Jr. asking for gold-standard placebo-controlled trials of the whole schedule.
units.framing_note: STANCE (T4-T5 only, 9th-grade level): the config framing: vaccines SCRUTINIZED, not celebrated, and not anti-vaccine. The immunology and smallpox's eradication are stated flatly as real; the institutional record (Cutter, the liability shield, under-reporting, the untested whole schedule) is stated as documented fact and attributed; consent is absolute; the dissenters are presented as demanding better evidence, by name; 'anti-vaxxer' is never used. No sermon either way; no claim the bank cannot source.

units.title: When the State Decides the Science
units.scope: Science bent by power, and the evidence it ignored: Trofim Lysenko, backed by Stalin, rejected genetics in the Soviet Union; geneticists were jailed or shot, and Nikolai Vavilov, who had built one of the world's great seed collections to fight famine, died starving in prison in 1943; Lysenko's farming methods failed; eugenics, the claim that society should breed out the 'unfit', was taught as science in the early 1900s: Indiana's 1907 sterilisation law, the Supreme Court's Buck v. Bell (1927, upholding the sterilisation of Carrie Buck, never formally overturned), some 20,000 sterilisations in California; the Nuremberg Code (1947) and consent; the lesson that a scientific claim stands on evidence, not on who backs it.
units.framing_note: STANCE (T4-T5 only, 9th-grade level): dark chapters and state-enforced science in full honesty, at a 9th-grade level: name who did it; one clause of harm, no gore; keep to the science that was ignored or abused (genetics, evidence, consent); the court and party politics are the history bank's.

units.title: The COVID Record, Weighed
units.scope: What the evidence showed after the 2020 pandemic, attributed claim by claim: the Great Barrington Declaration (October 2020) by Jay Bhattacharya, Martin Kulldorff and Sunetra Gupta urged protecting the old and vulnerable while letting the young live normally, and was dismissed by top officials (Francis Collins asked for a 'quick and devastating' takedown, in emails later released); Sweden kept most schools open; school closures and their documented learning losses; a 2023 Cochrane review found masks made little or no clear difference in community trials; infection gave lasting immunity (natural immunity); the lab-leak hypothesis, first called a conspiracy theory, later judged most likely by the FBI and the US Energy Department; Bhattacharya became director of the National Institutes of Health in 2025.
units.framing_note: STANCE (T4-T5 only, 9th-grade level): the config framing on COVID, at a 9th-grade level: dissent honoured and the dissenters named; every claim attributed and dated, every figure sourced; no pathogen detail of any kind (no genome, no engineering); steel-man the officials' reasons in an uncertain emergency; present, never preach; no cartoon villains. Keep to the evidence and the method; the politics are the history bank's.
